1: He was overcome by pity and despairing, his troubled eyes full of tears. To him, as he was, the slayer of Madhu spoke these words.
2: Where has this faintness of spirit come from, Arjuna, to fall on you in a hard hour? It is not the way of the noble. It does not lead to heaven, and it brings disgrace.
3: Do not give way to unmanliness at all, son of Pṛthā. It does not suit you. Throw off this petty weakness of heart and stand up, scorcher of foes.
4: Slayer of Madhu, how shall I fight back with arrows in battle against Bhīṣma and against Droṇa? Both of them are worthy of worship, slayer of enemies.
5: For it would be better to eat even begged food here in this world than to kill the teachers, men of great dignity. But if I killed the teachers, eager for gain as they are, I would be eating, right here, pleasures smeared with blood.
6: And we do not know which would weigh more for us: that we should conquer them, or that they should conquer us. The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are standing in front of us, the very men we would not wish to go on living after killing.
7: My own nature is struck down by the fault of wretchedness, and my mind is confused about dharma. So I ask you: tell me for certain what would be better. I am your pupil. I have taken refuge in you, so instruct me.
8: For I do not see what would drive away this grief of mine, which dries up my senses, not even if I won a prosperous kingdom on earth with no rival, and even lordship over the gods.
9: Having spoken so to the lord of the senses, scorcher of foes, the lord of sleep said to Govinda: I will not fight. And indeed he fell silent.
10: There he was, despairing in the middle of the two armies, descendant of Bharata, and to him the lord of the senses, as if smiling, spoke these words.
11: You have been grieving for those who should not be grieved for, and you speak words of wisdom. The learned do not grieve for those whose breath has gone, or for those whose breath has not.
12: But there was never a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these lords of men. And none of us will ever cease to exist from now on.
13: Just as the embodied one has childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it comes to have another body. The steadfast person is not confused about that.
14: But the contacts of the senses with their objects, son of Kuntī, bring cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Endure them, descendant of Bharata.
15: For the person whom these do not disturb, bull among men, who is steadfast and the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for deathlessness.
16: What is not has no being, and what is has no non-being. But the seers of the truth have seen the end of both of these.
17: But know that what pervades all this is indestructible. No one is able to bring about the destruction of this imperishable one.
18: These bodies are said to come to an end. They belong to the embodied one, who is eternal, indestructible and immeasurable. Therefore fight, descendant of Bharata.
19: Whoever knows this one as the slayer, and whoever thinks this one is slain: neither of the two understands. This one does not slay and is not slain.
20: It is never born and it never dies. Having been, it will never again cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
21: Take a person who knows this one to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and undecaying. How, son of Pṛthā, and whom, does that person cause to be slain? Whom does that person slay?
22: Just as a person casts off worn out clothes and takes others that are new, so the embodied one casts off worn out bodies and goes on to others that are new.
23: Weapons do not cut it and fire does not burn it. Water does not wet it and the wind does not dry it.
24: It cannot be cut, it cannot be burned, it cannot be wetted, and indeed it cannot be dried. It is eternal, it reaches everywhere, it stands firm, unmoving and primeval.
25: It is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable and unchangeable. So, knowing it to be this, you should not grieve over it.
26: And even if you think of it as constantly born, or constantly dead, even so, mighty-armed one, you should not grieve like this.
27: For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died. So you should not grieve over what cannot be avoided.
28: Beings are unmanifest at their beginning, manifest in their middle, descendant of Bharata, and unmanifest indeed at their end. What is there to lament in that?
29: One person sees it as a wonder. In just the same way another speaks of it as a wonder, and another hears of it as a wonder. And even after hearing, no one at all knows it.
30: This embodied one in the body of everyone can never be slain, descendant of Bharata. So you should not grieve for any being.
31: And looking at your own dharma too, you should not waver. For nothing better can be found for a warrior than a battle that accords with dharma.
32: And a battle such as this, son of Pṛthā, which has come by chance, is an open door to heaven. It is happy warriors who get one.
33: Now if you will not fight this battle, which accords with dharma, then you will have abandoned your own dharma and your fame, and you will incur evil.
34: People will also tell of your disgrace, and it will never fade. And for one who has been honoured, disgrace is worse than death.
35: The great chariot warriors will think you withdrew from the battle out of fear. They have held you in high esteem, and you will come to count for little with them.
36: And those who wish you ill will say many things that should not be said, and pour blame on your ability. What could be more painful than that?
37: Either you will be slain and reach heaven, or you will conquer and enjoy the earth. So stand up, son of Kuntī, resolved on battle.
38: Treat pleasure and pain as the same, and gain and loss, and victory and defeat, and then make yourself ready for battle. In this way you will not incur evil.
